Beyond the tooling limitation, I'd also flag that this command is worth double-checking before you run it yourself:

- **`echo "ALL" > /etc/at.allow`** — Unlike `hosts.allow`, the `at.allow` file does **not** interpret `ALL` as a wildcard. It expects one username per line. Writing `ALL` would restrict `at`/`batch` usage to a literal user named "ALL" (which almost certainly doesn't exist), effectively locking everyone except root out of `at`.
- **`rm -f /etc/at.deny`** — Removing this is fine on its own, but combined with the above, the result is the opposite of what "ALL" suggests: no one can use `at`.

If your goal is to **allow everyone** to use `at`, you typically want:
```sh
rm -f /etc/at.allow /etc/at.deny
```
(With neither file present, behavior depends on the distro — some allow all users, others restrict to root. To explicitly allow all non-root users, leave an empty `/etc/at.deny`.)

If your goal is to **restrict `at` to root only**, then:
```sh
: > /etc/at.allow && rm -f /etc/at.deny
```
(an empty `at.allow` denies everyone not listed).

Let me know which behavior you're aiming for and I can give you the exact command to run.
